newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania fund boss pledges faster privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Romania fund boss pledges faster privatisation.

text.p: The new boss of Romania's main privatisation agency vowed on Tuesday to speed up privatisation in the ex-communist country and attract badly-needed foreign investment.
"Our number one target this year is the promotion of real reform. The pace of privatisation must pick up," said Sorin Dimitriu, president of the State Ownership Fund (FPS).
His remarks came shortly after a recently reshuffled FPS board elected him president of the privatisation agency.
"Attracting foreign investment is a part of our strategy as real privatisation in Romania is possible only with foreign capital," Dimitriu said.
The FPS, which has been handling privatisations since 1992, has been frequently criticised for delaying sell-offs and for privatisation irregulaties.

A Court of Account report on such alleged irregularities last month triggered a reshuffle of the agency, with parliament, the government and the presidency replacing their total 17 members on its board in what the former ruling leftists called "political cleansing".
Romania is now ruled by a centrist coalition, which also holds a majority in parliament.
Dimitriu, a member of the National Peasant Party, the backbone of the coalition, replaces Emil Dima, a senator for the former ruling Party of Social Democracy.
"Romania needs true investors, handling their own capital rather than banking credits," Dimitriu said.
Analysts say low domestic capital and thin foreign investor interest have been behind slow privatisation in Romania.
Direct foreign investment in seven years since the fall of communism stood at a little over $2.0 billion at end-1996, far lower than elsewhere in Eastern Europe.

The thin offer of attractive companies, including utilities, the high price of the equities slated for selloff, as well as unclear rules on foreign ownership of land have been cited as some of the reasons behind the low foreign investment.
"Foreign investors must fully hold a title deed for land," Dimitriu said.

His remark coincides with a move by parliament's upper house the Senate on Tuesday to pass a bill granting foreigners investing in Romania the right to own land. -- Luli Popescu, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
